title: Agents
intro.1: Give an agent a token, and it starts its own sessions and drives them, over MCP or plain HTTP. You watch any of them from the admin page and take over when you want.
mcp-on-the-server.title: MCP on the server
mcp-on-the-server.1: The installer offers easi.run to Claude Code with this line; once its summary says MCP is ready, easi.run is in Claude Code from its next session. It is the line for any MCP client that runs a command (stdio), here or from another computer over SSH, with the login you already use for the server in place of you@your-server:
mcp-on-the-server.2: admin mcp relays the client’s stdio to the running admin over a socket in its own state directory (mode 0600, answered only for the admin’s own user). No token, port or certificate is involved: whoever can run docker exec on the server can use it, and SSH carries it from another computer.
mcp-on-the-server.3: Its clients have an agent token’s rights, together: they start sessions and drive the ones they started, and the admin page shows those sessions like any token’s.
mcp-on-the-server.4: The same tools as below. ADMIN_LOCAL_MCP=0 turns the socket off; the public demo has none.
tokens.title: Tokens
tokens.1: Create one under Agent tokens on the admin page (or POST /api/tokens {"name"}). It is shown once: copy it then.
tokens.2: A token starts sessions and uses their desktop tools. It reaches only the sessions it started: never yours, another token’s, the viewer stream, downloads, takeovers, settings or tokens.
tokens.3: Requests carry it as Authorization: Bearer easi_…, with no cookie or CSRF token. A request from a page on another site (another Origin) is refused.
tokens.4: Revoking a token refuses it at once and stops every session it started, one still starting included.
tokens.5: A token’s sessions count toward ADMIN_MAX_SESSIONS, with yours: close them from the session list, or revoke the token, to free their places.
tokens.6: The admin keeps only each token’s SHA-256, in tokens.json in its state volume. Up to 32 tokens; none in the public demo.
your-logins-for-an.title: Your logins for an agent
your-logins-for-an.1: A token, or the local MCP clients, may resume the persistent sessions you allow it. It then acts on those sites as you, logged in, and stopping the session saves it again.
your-logins-for-an.2: list_saved_sessions (or GET /api/agent/saved-sessions) lists them as saved sessions; pass one’s id as resume to start_session. Any other answers “no such saved session”.
mcp-over-https.title: MCP over HTTPS
mcp-over-https.1: For clients that connect over HTTP with a token, the endpoint is /mcp: Streamable HTTP, JSON answers, no session state. It serves MCP 2026-07-28 and, for clients that open with initialize, 2025-11-25 and 2025-06-18. With Claude Code (tested with 2.1.303):
mcp-over-https.3: start_session {url, egress?, resume?}: returns the session’s id and its watch_url; resume resumes a saved session.
mcp-over-https.5: list_saved_sessions: the saved sessions it may resume.
mcp-over-https.6: The driver’s desktop tools (The agent lists them), each taking {session, arguments}, its own arguments under arguments.
http-api.title: HTTP API
http-api.4: A session’s agent runs one call at a time; The agent says how many may wait, and for how long.
when-you-take-over.title: When you take over
when-you-take-over.1: Open the session from its watch_url (it logs you in first) or from the session list. If nobody holds control and your agent is not using the session (no call running, none ended in the last 30 seconds), you usually hold control as it opens; otherwise you watch and take it with the control (cursor) button in the session’s bar. The agent lists every case.
when-you-take-over.2: While you hold control, its desktop tools are refused (409 over HTTP, isError over MCP; controlled says so), and they work again when you give it back. The agent says what a takeover does to its calls and results.
when-you-take-over.3: The tools are the ones a session without DevTools runs, pinned from the driver’s own definitions. Sessions a token starts never have DevTools.
route.post-api-agent-sessions: {url, egress?, resume?}: starts a session, through an egress by its name (refused with 424 {reason, detail} when its check fails), or with resume, resumes the saved session of that id this token may use (with no egress named, through the one its last session left through: refused with 409 if that egress is gone); returns it with its watch_url and saved_session (the one it resumed, or null).
route.get-api-agent-saved-sessions: The saved sessions this token may resume: id, name, running; and whether they are unlocked.
route.get-api-agent-sessions-id: One of them: its URL, controlled (a person holds it), failed, watch_url.
route.get-api-agent-tools: The desktop tools, as the driver defines them.
route.post-api-agent-sessions-id-tools-t: The body is the tool’s arguments; the answer is its MCP result.
